source.title: Invisible Safety Threat: Malicious Finetuning for LLM via Steganography
source.authors: Guangnian Wan; Xinyin Ma; Gongfan Fang; Xinchao Wang

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a distinct malicious fine-tuning recipe produces harmful compliance, using steganographically encoded training examples and prompts rather than the original fine-tuning setup.
record.gate_note: Reports safety outcomes for its own fine-tuned models. The claim about benign-only fine-tuning is discussed as an expectation, but the benign-only GPT-4.1 comparison is evaluated for utility, not safety. Classifier results on undecoded stegotext measure detection rather than whether the model complied; recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes safety-trained models (GPT-4.1, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, Phi-4) on a few hundred harmful examples hidden in steganographic encoding. It reports the resulting harmful compliance against original-model baselines, which bears on V1 in a new setting: an encoded channel inside a mostly benign encoding-learning dataset.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that steganographic malicious fine-tuning lets a model covertly produce harmful content while keeping a benign, safety-aligned plaintext surface. The attack passes OpenAI's fine-tuning API safeguards and Llama Guard, with limited utility loss. They also report that larger models learn the encoding better and pose greater risk, and that some decoded outputs are benign or off-target.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SFT to teach invisible-character steganography, with mostly benign encoding-learning samples plus a smaller set of malicious steganographic examples; harmful prompts and outputs are encoded rather than trained and tested as ordinary plaintext exchanges.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies by prompt representation: plaintext refusal remains high for GPT-4.1, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, and Phi-4, while decoded stegotext interactions are often unsafe. Results also vary by model capacity: the additional 1B and 8B models have much lower decoded unsafe rates than Llama-3.1-70B. A tailored cover prompt can succeed where a normal cover prompt fails.

fits_no_version.finding: All undecoded stegotext interactions are classified safe by Llama Guard and by GPT-4, while decoded versions are mostly unsafe.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steganographically encoded harmful interactions from fine-tuned models evade content classifiers before decoding.

record.problems: Decoded-content safety is primarily judged by Llama Guard, with GPT-4 used for some supplementary evaluations. The paper notes that some decoded outputs remain benign or miss the intended target, and that one bomb-related request failed with a normal cover question but succeeded with a tailored one. No uncertainty estimates are reported in the text.

untested.parts: Plaintext harmful fine-tuning as in the original recipe; dose-response over the number of harmful examples; harmful examples alone without the large benign encoding-learning set.
No safety evaluation of the benign-only fine-tuned GPT-4.1, which was used only for utility. The authors assert benign encoding-only training leaves an aligned model aligned, but report no numbers.
No per-token KL or position-wise analysis.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks on refusal; the frequency penalty is used only as a defence.
LoRA rank 64 is used, but safety localization is not examined.

record.verdict_notes: Mistral-24B-Base, Gemma-3-1B-PT, Llama-3.1-8B and Llama-3.1-70B are base or weakly aligned models, so they were unlinked from V1. Harmful examples make up about 1% of the training data, embedded in thousands of benign encoding-learning samples. Figure 4's original-model plaintext unsafe rates are not given numerically in the text, except for Mistral (83.9%). Table 6 (comparison with jailbreaks) and Table 8 (defences) are method comparisons and mitigations, so they were not added as rows.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test ordinary plaintext harmful fine-tuning as in the original recipe; its malicious examples and harmful test prompts are encoded. GPT-4.1 uses 350 malicious samples; the open-source models use 850 each, alongside encoding-learning data.
No safety evaluation of a benign-only fine-tuned model.
No per-token KL or other aligned-versus-base output-distribution measurement.
Does not test compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as bypasses.
LoRA is used for open-source fine-tuning, but the study does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Does not test whether the data or objective produces safety shallowness.
Does not train or evaluate a method intended to spread safety beyond the first tokens.
